tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (cpp/src/distance.cpp NGram::ngram vs csharp/Distance.cs CalcNGram, workload in run.js), the compilers and flags are in cpp/Makefile and the results file's version and build-cmd fields, and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) is stated. Both sides pack the same 4-grams into each language's standard hash map at release settings, and -O3 -march=native C++ builds were compared too, so A stands (knucleotide precedent: idiomatic std::unordered_map against an idiomatic runtime hash table).

corrections.claimed_speedup: C#/JIT 0.516 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s and C++/Clang++ 0.877 s (prod, -O2). The best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s (C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.85 s), so C# is about 1.67x faster than C++/G++ prod and 1.59x faster than the best row (derived from page data). Other .NET rows also win, including NativeAOT builds with no JIT: C#/SC-JIT 0.475 s, C#/R2R 0.526 s, C#/AOT 0.609 s. F#/JIT 0.534 s and Julia/Default 0.58 s also win. Java/OpenJDK at 2.072 s is slower, and the C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still: best C/Clang/Fast 1.789 s, C/Clang prod 1.811 s. The timed loop is 100 iterations over 10 string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet), after 20 untimed warm-up iterations.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). 'prod' (headline rows): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 for C++. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) are passed only on the link line (LDFLAGS) while objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place. Managed side: dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128, 'dotnet build -c Release' (Optimize=true) run as 'dotnet Benchmark.dll' with default tiered JIT; the C#/AOT rows are NativeAOT with IlcInstructionSet=native and IlcOptimizationPreference=Speed; Julia 1.13.1 run as 'julia --project=. --threads=16 benchmark.jl' (Julia/Max adds -O3 --check-bounds=no --math-mode=fast); Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar'. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count) before the timed loop.
corrections.caveats: This is a container comparison more than a JIT one. .NET NativeAOT builds with no JIT (C#/AOT 0.609 s, C#/SC-AOT 0.61 s) also beat every C/C++ row, so the runtime-jit-beats-aot category fits poorly. The C++ side uses node-based std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int>, reserved to the string length, with the default identity hash and prime-modulo buckets. An open-addressing map would likely close the gap. The C version (uthash with one malloc per distinct gram) is about 2x slower than the C++ one. The C# side does slightly more work: Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes copies both strings on every call. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). Java does not share the win, so this is not a general JIT property. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite. From the sources: for each string pair the C++ code builds two node-based std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int>, with one heap allocation per distinct 4-gram (up to 10,000 per map, all freed on return) and a modulo by a prime bucket count on every lookup. .NET Dictionary<uint,int> keeps its entries in two flat arrays sized up front. This is a container and allocator effect, not JIT code quality: the C# NativeAOT rows, which use no JIT, also beat every C/C++ row.

notes: Confirm at A: the numbers match the results file row for row, and the metadata checks out (MIT, 41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, not a fork). Shortcomings to record: a container comparison (node-based std::unordered_map against a flat .NET Dictionary); not a JIT win, since C# NativeAOT also beats every C++ row (consider a category override such as string-and-text); a single run; a subjective, AI-assisted suite; headline C++ rows at -O2, though the -O3 rows also lose; LTO flags inert.

corrections.caveats: C heap bug: priority_queue_pop in c/src/graph_path.c compares the children with the stale root instead of the moved last element, so it stops at once and leaves that element at the root without sifting it down. A verifier transcription of the code pops out of order on random input. On this benchmark's input the C search still does the same pops, pushes and edge scans as C++ and C# (verifier simulation), so the C rows time the same search with a cheaper pop, but the code is not a correct priority queue. Not a JIT win: the .NET ReadyToRun (1.222 s) and NativeAOT (1.321 s) rows beat every C/C++ row, and so do Java (1.486 s) and Julia (1.458 s), so the runtime-jit-beats-aot category fits poorly. Heap work is small (about 24,000 pushes per search), while each search allocates and fills two 500,000-int arrays (4 MB in total), which probably dominates the time. The result therefore likely measures allocation and initialisation behaviour rather than search code. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The record's heap-arity explanation is not supported. A verifier simulation of the suite's graph shows std::priority_queue (binary), .NET PriorityQueue (4-ary) and the C heap doing identical work: 1,173 pops, 23,842 pushes and 25,625 edge scans per search. Every search, on the other hand, allocates and fills two 500,000-int arrays (g_score and best_f, 4 MB), so the time is probably dominated by allocation and initialisation. The gap is then most likely memory-management behaviour (glibc malloc/free of 2 MB blocks against .NET large-object-heap reuse), not JIT code generation. This is inference and was not measured. C# NativeAOT (1.321 s) and ReadyToRun (1.222 s) also beat every C/C++ row.

notes: Confirm at A: the numbers match the results file, and same work on both sides was verified by simulating the suite's graph (path 1,172 equals the checksum 1,406,400 over 1,200 runs including warm-up). Shortcomings to record: the heap explanation is unsupported (heap work is identical and small, and per-search 4 MB array allocation and fill likely dominate); not a JIT effect, since C# AOT and R2R also win; the C rows run a heap whose pop never sifts down; the baseline should be read as C++ (1.38x over the best C++ row); a single run; a subjective suite.

tier_reason: The harness meets A methodology (cpp/src/sort.cpp std::sort vs julia/src/benchmarks/Sort.jl sort!, flags in cpp/Makefile, versions and CPU in the results file) and the rows match. However, the two sides run different algorithms. For this Vector{Int32} (400,000 values in 0..999,999), Julia's default sort! dispatches to its LSD RadixSort per base/sort.jl, while std::sort runs introsort, so the language-level claim is capped at C (same_algorithm false precedent: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl, Julia matmul-no-blas).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Julia/Default 0.116 s vs C++/G++ 0.982 s (prod -O2, also the best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations), C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.998 s and C++/Clang++ 1.022 s: about 8.5x (derived from page data). Java/OpenJDK at 0.187 s is about 5.3x faster than std::sort (derived). C# Array.Sort at 1.057 s is slightly slower. The C rows use qsort with a comparison callback (best C/mycc/LLVM/Default 1.957 s, C/Gcc/Fast 1.964 s). The timed loop is 50 sorts of a copied 400,000-element array after 10 untimed warm-up sorts. The suite's same-algorithm sorts show no managed-runtime win: Sort::Quick Julia/Default 1.307 s vs C/Gcc 1.15 s, and Sort::Merge Julia/Default 1.602 s vs C/Clang 1.09 s.

corrections.caveats: Not the same algorithm. std::sort is a comparison introsort. Julia's default sort! for Int32 runs ComputeExtrema and skips counting sort because the range (about 1,000,000) exceeds half the length. It then picks its stable LSD RadixSort, because 20 bits + 70 < 22 ln(399,999), which is about 284 (base/sort.jl ConsiderRadixSort). The suite's own docs/ai_critic.js says 'You're comparing algorithms, not languages'. A radix sort in C++ would be expected to match or beat it. The Java row is probably not a JIT win either. OpenJDK ships an AVX2 sort intrinsic (libsimdsort, avx2-32bit-qsort.hpp, C++ based on Intel x86-simd-sort) that Arrays.sort(int[]) can use on AVX2 CPUs such as this Ryzen; whether it ran here was not checked. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithm choice in the standard library, not the language or the JIT. Julia's sort! dispatch (base/sort.jl _DEFAULT_ALGORITHMS_FOR_VECTORS: ComputeExtrema, ConsiderCountingSort, ConsiderRadixSort) selects an O(n) LSD radix sort for 400,000 Int32 values with a 20-bit range, while std::sort runs an O(n log n) comparison introsort. The suite's docs/ai_analysis.js and docs/ai_critic.js attribute the win to radix sort too.

notes: Downgrade A to C: the numbers match the results file, but the win is Julia's standard-library radix sort against comparison-based std::sort (same_algorithm false). It is an algorithm win, not a language win, and the same-algorithm Sort::Quick and Sort::Merge tests show C ahead. Shortcomings to record: different algorithm; the Java row is likely the JDK's x86-simd-sort intrinsic; a single run; a subjective suite. Consider a category override out of runtime-jit-beats-aot (for example numerics-and-arrays).
